One spec, three formats

One spec, three formats

A single Python spec emits MJCF, URDF and SDF. Link geometry, mass, inertia and joint limits are computed once, never typed twice.

Validated two ways: 151 property comparisons across the three files, then an independent NumPy forward-kinematics implementation checked against MuJoCo's own over 2000 random configurations.

151/151properties agree
3.3e-16max FK error m
2000configs checked
The files agreed with themselves

The first emitter passed all 147 numeric checks and still had a 0.23 m forward-kinematics error. MJCF size is a half extent; URDF and SDF box size is the full extent. Every property matched because each format was being compared against itself.

Reproducibility

Reproducibility

Repeated runs are bit-identical. So is a re-parsed model. Adding an untouched body three metres away changes nothing.

What bounds reproducibility is chaos. Two perturbation sizes recover the same exponent, and the exponent fitted on one run blind-predicts the other.

9.178spredicted 1mm
9.7225smeasured
1.2%seeds agree
6.5xcontact slower
Two floating-point traps

A one-ULP nudge of 2.22e-16 added to a coordinate of 2.0 — whose ULP is twice that — rounds away entirely. The runs came out bit-identical and read as no chaos.

And nextafter(0,1) is the smallest denormal, which produced a meaningless 2e305x growth figure.

model/determinism.py

Friction has the shape of a square

Friction has the shape of a square

Coulomb friction confines the tangential force to a circle. The common approximation uses a polygon — and the polygon shows.

Error is zero at 0, 45 and 90 degrees — the square's symmetry axes — and peaks between them. Eight lobes around the circle.

12.76dpyramidal worst
0.71delliptic worst
2.6xelliptic faster
What I got wrong, in my own docstring

I called the pyramid the cheaper option. It is 2.6x slower as well as 18x less accurate — dominated on both axes.

Verify the order, not the vibe

Verify the order, not the vibe

A method of order p has global error O(dt^p), so the slope of a log-log plot is the order. All four land on theirs.

Then the ranking reverses. With a stiff velocity actuator — a joint PD controller's derivative term — RK4 is less stable than Euler.

isfinite() is not a stability test

The first sweep called Euler stable at kv=500 after it failed at 20, 50 and 100. MuJoCo detects a diverged step and resets the state to zero — it hit |qvel|=3.45e5, got reset, then sat at exactly zero for 397 steps. Perfectly finite, perfectly meaningless.

model/integrators.py

both stable
LIVE, and a reduced model: one rotational DOF, not the measured system. Explicit Euler (red) applies the damping force using the OLD velocity, so past kv·dt/I = 2 the correction overshoots and compounds. The implicit form (blue) solves for the new velocity and cannot. Push the gain past about 100.

Two engines, two shapes of failure

Two engines, two shapes of failure

The same experiment in MuJoCo and PhysX. They agree on something non-obvious: penetration is invariant to a 1000x mass change in each.

They disagree on everything else. MuJoCo is flat until 2*dt passes its 0.02s time constant. PhysX has no constant to clamp.

2155xsofter at 480Hz
61xsofter at 60Hz
37xPhysX jump
Right answer, unverified reasoning

Both predictions were confirmed. One of the two reasons was not: I attributed PhysX's mass independence to the rest offset, but rest_offset read 0.0 for the entire sweep.

model/crossengine_contact.py

A cliff, not a curve

A cliff, not a curve

In MuJoCo, solver iterations never help a bad mass ratio — 1 and 50 give identical results.

In PhysX they help, but as a step function: 1, 32 and 64 are indistinguishable failures and 96 is a working stack.

64>96where it flips
0velocity iters help
255still fails at 1e4
The control that named the mechanism

Velocity iterations at 1, 32, 128 and 255 all leave it at ~100mm. So the cliff is not about total solver effort — it is specifically position-level depenetration work. That turns a correlation into a mechanism.

model/crossengine_stack.py

STACK HOLDS
Four real runs. The light block is 1 kg throughout; only the block on top changes. PhysX fails between 10 and 100, MuJoCo degrades gradually — the charts above measure both.

A grip force nobody supplied

A grip force nobody supplied

A parallel-jaw grasp holds when 2*mu*F >= m*g. Friction and mass go in; the holding threshold comes out of the dynamics.

All four land above the closed form, and the sign is the point. A measurement below theory would mean the contact model invents friction the materials do not license.

+7.5%mean excess
0.37Nadditive offset
4xtighter than rel.
Testing the explanation, not asserting it

The excess could be proportional or additive. Absolute excess clusters at 0.313 / 0.451 / 0.331 / 0.368 N with a coefficient of variation of 0.144, against 0.598 for the relative reading. Additive wins by 4x.

Eleven attempts, then a trot

Eleven attempts, then a trot

A trot has one signature: diagonal pairs move together, and the two pairs are half a cycle apart.

Ten attempts measured in the world frame and kept describing a robot falling over. The eleventh changed the frame: a gait generator's output is the foot trajectory relative to the trunk.

0.0dFL+HR apart
4.8dFR+HL apart
177.6dbetween pairs
4.8dworst dev.
One robot of three, and the others are diagnosed

ANYmal: two of four legs resolved to a shank rather than a foot, so the tracked points sit partway up the chain. A1: the legs never moved at all — 1e-5 m of excursion.

The error that cost the most named the wrong subsystem. An if sat outside the stepping loop, so the sim was never stepped and the arrays stayed empty — surfacing as zero-size array to reduction. I read that as foot detection failing and rewrote foot detection twice.

model/gait_result.py

Reading friction back out

Reading friction back out

mu goes into PhysX as a material property. The angle at which a block slides comes out of the dynamics. tan(theta) = mu closes the loop.

Three coefficients recovered to better than 2% — without ever asking the engine what friction it was using.

+1.9%mu 0.3
+1.9%mu 0.5
+1.2%mu 0.8
0.435dmax overshoot
My prediction was wrong in DIRECTION

I predicted a low bias, reasoning that pre-slip creep would trip the detector early. But the sweep steps in 2-degree increments, so the first angle flagged can only ever be the first grid line at or above the threshold. The bias had to be positive.

Creep is there in the data — 0.4 to 0.8 mm one step before release — it just never reaches the detection threshold.

model/friction_recovery.py

What URDF cannot say

What URDF cannot say

URDF is a tree: one parent per link. Four-bar linkages, parallel jaws and differential drives are outside the format's data model.

Drop the closure and the mechanism still simulates, still looks plausible, and is half dead — the rocker travels 0.0000 rad.

0.0000open rocker rad
0.7191closed rocker rad
109xtuning the closure
Wrong diagnosis, then the correction

A 57mm worst-case gap looked like a soft constraint. Stiffening moved the mean 109x and the max barely at all — because the max is at step 0. The model was spawned 60.7mm off the constraint manifold.

model/closed_chain.py

The metric measured the wrong thing

The metric measured the wrong thing

Raw throughput says a 282-vertex hull is 11.8x slower than the sphere it approximates. But the scenes do not generate the same number of contacts.

Per contact, the box is cheaper than the sphere — it only looked slow because it makes four times the contacts.

~5xcost per 23.5x hull
sub-linhull scaling
A gate that guards its own confound

A CI test asserts the box stays cheaper per contact, so the “raw steps/s is the wrong metric” argument fails loudly if its own example ever inverts.

model/collision_cost.py

The stiffness you asked for is not the one you got

The stiffness you asked for is not the one you got

MuJoCo parameterises contact softness in time, not stiffness — and silently clamps the requested time constant to twice the timestep.

Ask for a contact stiffer than your timestep supports and you quietly get the softer one. No warning is emitted. This finding turned up again, independently, in two later studies.

0.1078mm, tc=0.0001
0.1078mm, tc=0.02
flatacross 1000x mass
I predicted penetration would scale with load

It does not. The solver normalises by the contact's effective mass, so the load cancels exactly — 0.1078 mm at 0.1 kg and at 100 kg. The prediction is kept in the source next to the measurement that refuted it, because the reason it fails is the interesting part.

model/contact_tuning.py

Rotor inertia reflects as N squared

Rotor inertia reflects as N squared

The gearbox term everyone drops. A rotor's inertia appears at the joint multiplied by the square of the gear ratio.

At N=100, a 2e-5 kg·m² rotor contributes more inertia than the entire link it drives. Four actuator models validated against closed-form torque, all to 0.00% error.

0.00%torque error
2.3xrotor vs link at N=100
A 196% discrepancy that was mine

I reported a large simulator disagreement that turned out to be a sign error in my own torque expression, plus a thin-rod inertia used for a capsule — 4.3% off. The gate now asks MuJoCo for the body inertia rather than assuming it.

model/actuators.py

The parameter you cannot identify

The parameter you cannot identify

System identification over the same model. Three parameters recover; one has a trajectory sensitivity of exactly zero.

That is the honest answer, not a failure: the experiment carries no information about it, so no optimiser can recover it. Reporting a fitted value would be inventing one.

0.000damping_j1 sens.
3of 4 identifiable
35xbetter with true seed
Two hypotheses refuted in a row

I predicted richer excitation would improve the fit. It did not — 168.8% to 168.3%. I then concluded the parameters were unidentifiable, which was also wrong: seeding the optimiser with the true values fit 35x better, so the problem was a trapped optimiser, not missing information.

model/sysid.py

Newton, CG, PGS

Newton, CG, PGS

On a well-conditioned problem all three agree on the answer to 0.01 mm, which makes the speed difference free to take.

Newton is 14x faster than PGS — the classic game-physics choice — at identical accuracy.

14xNewton over PGS
0.01mmthey all agree to
No solver rescues a bad mass ratio

On the 1000:1 stack they only change WHICH body fails. Newton drives the light block 49 mm into the floor; CG and PGS let the heavy one pass entirely through it. Two different wrong answers, neither better. With the iteration sweep, that closes it: a bad mass ratio is not a solver-tuning problem at all.

model/solvers.py

Where the time actually goes

Where the time actually goes

A C++ harness against the same model, with MuJoCo's per-phase timers enabled. Collision detection costs roughly three times the constraint solver.

Which is why solver-iteration tuning was the wrong lever — something the stability study independently confirmed from the other direction.

284xrealtime, C++
26.9%collision
10.0%solve
MuJoCo's profiler is opt-in

Without installing mjcb_time the entire timer array reads zero — which looks exactly like every phase being free.

cpp/sim_bench.cpp

About this page

Every figure is generated from the measured JSON by tools/build_kare.py, so the charts cannot drift from the studies. A separate CI gate checks the repository README's prose against the same data — it has caught three hand-typed roundings so far.

Type is set the way the Macintosh set it: a chunky bitmap face for chrome and labels, a legible one for prose. Icons are 16x16, drawn a pixel at a time. The bomb is what a classic Mac showed when something went wrong, which is why it marks the corrections.

Sixteen of the nineteen studies have a window here. The other three are folded in rather than dropped: the ten failed gait attempts sit inside the trot window, and the stability-frontier sweep supplies the mass-ratio and iteration charts in two windows above. All nineteen are in the repository.

One honest gap in the results themselves: the trot validates on Spot and not on ANYmal or A1, and both failures are diagnosed rather than smoothed over.
